title: Onboarding — from “they're in” to active
objective: Take a squad from the moment somebody decides a person is in, to the day the club stops chasing them for anything: three arrival doors, one welcome, one signed link carrying one questionnaire, a checklist the club can see and resolve, a bounded chase that gives up and tells a human, and a human declaration that makes them active.
why_now: Mission 6 fills the top of the funnel and Mission 5 shipped the record and the board that display all of this, deliberately undeployed — LAN-196 holds Missions 5, 6 and 7 for one release window, so this is the last of a set that ships together. Until it exists there is no path from a recruit or a spreadsheet to a season's squad except an operator typing, and no consent capture outside the recruit door, which means the club cannot lawfully message anybody it did not meet at a recruiting event. Two shipped things also depend on it to become coherent: Mission 5's operator correction path was accepted only as the interim answer until a person can fix their own record, and its missing-data queue has nothing acting on it today.
non_goals: Consent wording, retention, correction policy, subject-access export, erasure and under-18 handling — Mission 8; the wording is Clint's through Task 07.
Creating a season, season rollover, and the season-boundary checklist reset — Mission 11.
The recruitment funnel, its doors and its ladder up to the flip — Mission 6.
Any chase of a recruit at all.
All coach and committee onboarding, welcome flow included, and football assignments — Mission 9.
The Monday report's own evolution — Mission 10.
Real data, hosted cutover and production activation — Tracks A and B; LAN-86, LAN-101, LAN-126.
Per-season configuration of which checklist items exist, and per-item owners — superseded by Brian on 2026-09-02.

requirements.text: Three arrival doors — a CSV import of last season's squad, an operator adding one person by hand, and a recruit flipped to joined — and what happens after them is identical: a season membership at onboarding, the season's checklist generated in full, and one welcome.
One welcome template for everybody, which does not vary by door. It is the only message the club may send before a messaging basis exists, and its purpose is to obtain one.

One signed, revocable, season-scoped link per person, carrying no session and exposing nobody else's information. At most one open ask per person, ever: new outstanding facts join the open ask rather than starting a second. There are no player logins in any form.

One questionnaire behind that link, in five steps: the player's details, the Code of Conduct, the photo release, BUCS Play, and Hudl. Every later message re-sends the same link, compiled to whatever is still outstanding.

The personal-details form is the consent board. The tick is its first field, not a preamble. Consent is season-scoped and re-asked every season; within a season a recruit-door grant carries, so nobody is asked twice in one year.
Consent is one-way on the player's side: their own form offers no way to untick it. An operator can switch it off at any point, on request, as part of the person's status.

The onboarding required set is person-required.ts's player tier — first name, last name, mobile, personal email, college, matriculation year, expected graduation, degree field, date of birth and an emergency contact of first name, last name, email and phone. It blocks the form and never the player, and whatever a step saved stays saved. Declining a required fact is not offered anywhere.

Nothing gates. No onboarding item blocks any action anywhere, for anybody. An active player with an unfinished checklist is the normal case, not an exception. Onboarding memberships count as players for event audiences from the moment they are on the team.
The checklist is the approved item-and-ask inventory. Nobody configures which items exist, per season or otherwise, and no item has a per-item owner: only the four-role group resolves anything.

Checklist item states are pending, invited, claimed, complete, waived and not_applicable, with reopen from any terminal state. claimed means the player says done and awaits confirmation; a trust-class item completes on the player's word carrying player-claimed provenance. Verification class is a property of the item, not a configuration knob.

Waive and reopen are four-role actions requiring no reason, audited, with the author recorded. This supersedes the shipped onboarding_items_waiver_is_justified constraint, which must be unwound by a forward-only migration.
Per-item history is append-only: a superseded value is retained, never overwritten, and every state transition records actor, date and the state pair.

A per-player activity log, grouped by section, carrying one entry per ask and per answer with when, how and who — so the record answers how often somebody was asked about a thing, not merely whether they were messaged.

A player's answer never silently overwrites a value an operator recorded, an externally verified value, or a derived one. It raises disputed — awaiting verification, both values are kept, and a four-role operator decides. Provenance is the derived one Mission 5 already built from audit_events.
requirements.note: Q-9 (Brian, 2026-09-04, in the mission journal): 'I don't think the disputed fact mechanism survives at all. I think that gets gone.' No disputed state, no second contested value, no four-role resolve control. The rule is last-write-wins: a player's answer overwrites directly, and the audit history already rendered on the person record carries who changed what and when. Kept here, superseded rather than deleted, as the record of what was originally required and why it changed.

requirements.text: A player fixes their own record through the same signed link, at any time. This is the club's whole answer to self-service and replaces Mission 5's operator correction path as the interim answer.

The chase is configured as three values on the messaging schedule's Onboarding section: how long after joining the first chase goes, how many times it asks, and how far apart. There is no separate give-up value; the chase ends when the count runs out. There are no quiet hours.

The count is spent only on messages known to have arrived. A delivery failure consumes nothing and routes to the failure path, which puts the person on the list for a human and sends no automated email in its place. LAN-93 delivery callbacks are a stated dependency.

An operator nudges one person or several from the queue in one action, each receiving only their own compiled ask on their own link. Operator nudges are unlimited and outside the count. The system never generates a one-fact ask of its own.

The queue shows, per person, when they were last contacted and what kind it was, and when the machine will next write or that it will not — distinguishing exhausted, unmessageable and terminal delivery failure.

When the count runs out the chase stops permanently and escalates to a configured office, initial value President, read from the club's roles rather than configured. The escalation carries a count and a link and never names. Only a human restarts a chase. No automated timeout ever removes anybody.

Activation is a human declaration by the four-role group on the shipped status field, with no confirmation step. It completes, waives and closes nothing, and derived onboarding-completeness is display-only and never flips membership on its own.

Date of birth is restricted: it never appears on any list, board or queue, and only the derived under-18 flag does. A person flagged under 18 is not messaged at all until a fresh owner decision defines under-18 handling. Free text — refusal notes, correction reasons, waiver reasons — is four-role only and never reaches a report verbatim.

Every player-facing screen shows the club's privacy policy at the point of collection, and the Code of Conduct and photo release are read on their own pages before being agreed, each recorded against the exact version shown and dated.
Nothing is ever sent by hand. Every message rides Mission 4's pipeline, template-only in production, and the refuse-without-basis check permits only the welcome before a basis exists.
Leaving mid-onboarding simply stops the ask. Nothing more is asked, the person drops off the queue, and whatever records exist stay as they are.

decisions.id: W1:The file carries first name, last name and mobile — required
decisions.text: The file carries first name, last name and mobile — required — plus personal email, college and matriculation year, optional. Nothing else.
decisions.basis: Those three are the required set at every tier and are what a welcome needs to arrive. The other three are things a club spreadsheet genuinely holds and that save the player retyping. Everything else onboarding asks for — DOB, emergency contact, degree, graduation — comes from nowhere on main, is asked of everyone anyway, and does not belong in a file on a laptop.

decisions.id: W1:A carried-forward person's own facts are never overwritten b
decisions.text: A carried-forward person's own facts are never overwritten by the file. A difference becomes something the player confirms on the form, not a silent update.
decisions.basis: The mission's standing rule that nothing a person says silently overwrites a confirmed value (W5) reads the same way pointed at a spreadsheet. The alternative — last-file-wins over a value a human confirmed — is the failure mode the whole provenance design exists to prevent. Recommended.

workflow_matrix.entry_point: The roster board — the surface an operator already works from.
workflow_matrix.placement: `/operate/roster/import`, reached from an **Add players** menu on the roster board. The Events page already carries a menu of exactly this shape (`src/app/operate/events/create-menu.tsx`), added by LAN-155 so that bulk import could sit beside the single-record path without displacing it.
actions: Open the import. From the roster board's Add players menu. The screen
Download the template. The event import ships a prompt and a versioned
Choose a file. Refused whole, before any row is read, if it is over the
Read the proposal. One table, one row per line of the file, each row
Confirm. One action. Everything that can apply applies; refused rows are
Read what happened. Counts by outcome, the names that arrived, the rows
Abandon, at any point before confirming. Nothing is written.

Tick consent — where it is asked. One-way: the control that grants it
Confirm or correct each pre-filled value; fill each gap, including the
Save and continue.

workflow_matrix.title: Settle a disputed fact
workflow_matrix.retired_note: Q-9 (Brian, 2026-09-04, in the mission journal): 'I don't think the disputed fact mechanism survives at all. I think that gets gone.' This workflow does not ship, in any form. What ships instead: a player's answer overwrites the operator-recorded value directly (last write wins), and the person record's own audit history — who changed what, and when — is what the operator reads. Kept here as the record of what was originally approved and why it was withdrawn, not as live behaviour.
workflow_matrix.trigger: a fact goes to `disputed — awaiting verification` when a player's answer differs from an operator-recorded value (`W5`).
workflow_matrix.entry_point: **`/operate/people/[personId]`**, the person record, which ships. Reached from the missing-data queue, the roster, or a link in the chase.
workflow_matrix.placement: **`/operate/people/[personId]`**, the person record, which ships. Reached from the missing-data queue, the roster, or a link in the chase.
actions: Open a person with a disputed fact.
Read both values, both attributions, and the history.
Resolve: keep the club's value, or take the player's.
Optionally record why — free text, four-role only, never in a report.
workflow_matrix.user_visible_result: one value stands, the other is retained, and the record says who decided and when.

Select one person, or several.
Nudge. Each selected person receives their own compiled ask.

They see the people whose chase has exhausted, with what each is missing and
They contact one of them themselves — in person, or by phone.
They record what happened on that person's log.

permitted_clarifications: Naming, placement and layout detail that changes no approved meaning, and follows the shipped surface the screen was photographed on.
Which existing component satisfies an approved screen, provided nothing new is drawn and the reused component's own idiom is kept.
How the fifteen asks are grouped into sections, and whether a document opens in place or on its own sub-page.
Field-level validation and error wording beyond the shipped BUSY_MESSAGE.
Test structure, fixture shape and the synthetic universe's contents, provided no real person or club record appears.
How the chase's three values are stored, and where the escalation office is read from.
requires_packet_revision: Any change to the required set, or to required blocking the form rather than the player.
Introducing a way for a player to decline a required fact, or a system-generated one-fact ask.
Any weakening of nothing-gates, or making any onboarding item block any action anywhere.
Any change to one-open-ask-per-person, or issuing a second live link to one person in one season.
Making consent removable by the player, or askable more than once per season.
Configuring which checklist items exist, or assigning an item to an owner other than the four-role group.
Putting a name, a count per person, or item detail into the exhaustion escalation.
Adding a confirmation step to activation.
